h1: Working in brewery supply chain and planning
title: Working in Brewery Supply Chain | Craft Beer School
desc: What brewery supply chain and planning roles involve: buying, forecasting, production schedules, stock and logistics. How to start.
teaser: Behind every pint is a planner who bought the malt on time. Here is what the job involves.
standfirst: Supply chain and planning keep a brewery running. This guide describes the work, the numbers and the routes in for people who like logistics more than tasting.
sections:
A brewery has to buy raw materials, brew on a schedule, package, store and deliver, all against a forecast of what customers will buy. Supply chain and planning is the team that ties these together. They decide how much to brew, when, in which tank and which pack. They make sure the malt, hops, cans and labels arrive on time.

In a small brewery one person may do this alongside other jobs. In a larger one it is a department with buyers, planners and logistics staff.

The work is rarely visible when it goes well. Nobody toasts the planner when the right cans arrive on Tuesday, but everyone notices when they do not.

Buyers source malt, hops, yeast, packaging, cleaning chemicals and spare parts. They compare suppliers on price, quality, lead time and reliability. Hops and specialty malts may come from other continents, so lead times can run to weeks or months and prices can move with harvests and freight. Brewers care about the specification as much as the price: a malt with the wrong colour or moisture is not a bargain.

A good buyer asks for certificates of analysis and keeps a second supplier for critical items. Read the beer styles guide to see why the spec matters.

Planning begins with a forecast: how much of each beer will sell, by week, by pack. The planner turns that into a brew schedule. Constraints are real: a lager tank is occupied for weeks, a hoppy beer should reach customers fresh. A seasonal beer sells for a short window. Plan too little and you run out. Plan too much and old beer is poured away.

Tank capacity is the main bottleneck in many craft breweries. A planner works out which beer goes into which fermenter, when it is ready and when the tank can be cleaned for the next brew.

A useful habit is a weekly planning meeting of fifteen minutes with the head brewer, the packaging lead and sales. Each person says what is changing. Most stock-outs trace back to a conversation that did not happen.
Stock, shelf life and the cold chain

Beer is a perishable product, so stock rotation matters. Planners track best-before dates and push the oldest stock first. In hot climates cold storage and chilled transport protect flavour, but they cost money. Decide which beers need chilled distribution and which can travel at ambient temperature. See can or bottle for hot markets.

Packaging materials have long lead times too. Printed cans can take weeks to arrive and are ordered in large minimums. A planner who forgets to order cans stops the line.

Planners live in spreadsheets and, in larger firms, planning systems. They track yield (the volume of saleable beer from each brew), loss, stock levels and service level, which means how often orders are delivered in full and on time. Comfort with data helps more than any specific software.

Excise or duty records and warehouse records often need to match. Rules differ by country, so learn the local requirements from your employer or a licensing adviser.

Keep a simple record of supplier delivery performance. If a hop merchant is late three times, you have evidence for a better contract or a second source.

Entry routes include roles in purchasing, warehouse, logistics, production planning or customer service at a brewery, distributor or other drinks company. People come from retail, manufacturing, transport and finance. Learn the basics of brewing so you understand lead times and constraints. A visit to a brewery on a brew day will teach you more than a week of reading.

See upskilling a brewery team online for how brewers train staff. See also how to become a brewer without a degree if you want to see the brewhouse side.

Planners move into operations management, procurement leadership or general management, because they see the whole business. We do not quote salaries and cannot promise outcomes; pay differs by country and company.

Understanding costs, pricing and the commercial side of a brewery helps in this field. Brewery Business Management is a three-week live online course that covers those foundations.
faqs: Do I need to brew to work in planning?
No, but you need to understand the process and its time constraints.
Spreadsheets first. Planning systems vary by employer.
Is this a good role for people who dislike sales?
Yes, if you enjoy organising, data and working with suppliers and production teams.
Often yes, with peaks before holidays and in warm months. Planners prepare for them months ahead.
